steps.say: Small kidney cancers are removed while the kidney stays in place. Partial nephrectomy is the preferred operation for T1a tumours of four centimetres or less and for feasible T1b tumours. Keeping nephrons preserves long term kidney function and lowers future cardiovascular risk.
steps.tx: **Partial nephrectomy** (nephron-sparing surgery) is the preferred standard for **T1a mass** lesions (renal tumours **4 cm or less**, four centimetres) and feasible T1b tumours, preserving long-term renal function. The tumour is excised with a thin rim of normal parenchyma and the defect reconstructed, trading longer operating time for a lifetime of better kidney function and lower cardiovascular risk.

vis.alt: Bisected nephrectomy specimen with a golden-yellow clear cell tumour.
vis.caption: Golden-yellow clear cell tumour of the type removed with a parenchymal margin. Credit: James Heilman, MD.

steps.say: Clamp time decides how much kidney survives. Warm ischaemia at body temperature must stay under twenty to twenty five minutes. Cold ischaemia with ice slush extends the safe window to thirty five minutes. Beyond these limits acute tubular necrosis sets in and the saved kidney never regains full function.
steps.tx: **Warm ischemia time** (arterial clamp time at body temperature) should stay under **20 to 25 minutes** (twenty to twenty five), while **cold ischemia** (ice slush cooling around the kidney) extends safety to **35 minutes** (thirty five). Beyond these limits irreversible acute tubular necrosis sets in and the preserved kidney never regains full function, so resection and renorrhaphy are planned against the clock.

vis.alt: Illustration of partial nephrectomy with clamped renal artery and clear cell histology.
vis.caption: Partial nephrectomy under hilar clamping keeps ischemia within safe limits. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Some tumours grow into the veins. Four to ten in a hundred cancers extend into the renal vein and vena cava. The Neves-Zincke system classifies the thrombus from level one in the renal vein to level four above the diaphragm. The level dictates the whole operative plan.
steps.tx: Renal cell carcinoma extends into the renal vein and vena cava as an **IVC thrombus** (tumour clot in the great vein) in **4% to 10%** (four to ten in a hundred) of cases, staged by the **Neves-Zincke classification** (thrombus level system) from Level I in the renal vein to Level IV above the diaphragm and atrium. The level dictates the entire plan, from caval milking to opening the chest, and must be mapped precisely on preoperative imaging.

rows: Renal vein only, caval milking suffices
Vena cava below diaphragm, vascular control and cavotomy
Above diaphragm into atrium, cardiac team needed

steps.say: Thrombus above the diaphragm needs a cardiac operation. The team uses bypass with deep cooling and circulatory arrest to open the vena cava in a bloodless field. A probe in the gullet follows the thrombus in real time. Cardiac surgery, anaesthesia, and urology act as one team.
steps.tx: Level IV thrombi above the diaphragm require **cardiopulmonary bypass** (heart-lung machine circulation) with deep **hypothermic circulatory arrest** (cooling plus total circulatory stop), while transesophageal echocardiography tracks the thrombus live. This operation needs three teams at once: cardiac surgery, anaesthesia, and urology acting as one unit.

rows: Deep hypothermia plus circulatory stop, bloodless field

steps.say: Metastatic disease is grouped by risk before drugs are chosen. The IMDC system uses six clinical factors, including performance status under eighty percent and less than a year from diagnosis to treatment. Patients with none of these factors have favourable risk, while the rest fall into intermediate or poor groups.
steps.tx: The **IMDC criteria** (International Metastatic RCC Database Consortium risk model) stratify metastatic RCC with **6 factors** (six clinical risk items): **Karnofsky performance** below **80%** (eighty percent), under **1 year** (one year) from diagnosis to treatment, anemia, hypercalcemia, neutrophilia, and thrombocytosis. Favourable-risk patients carry none, while intermediate and poor-risk patients carry at least one factor, and their group steers first-line therapy.

rows: None equals favourable, any equals intermediate or poor

steps.say: Intermediate and poor risk metastatic disease needs combination immunotherapy. Options pair two checkpoint drugs, nivolumab with ipilimumab, or a vessel blocking tablet with a PD-1 drug such as pembrolizumab. Combinations beat single drug sunitinib on survival, at the price of immune side effects that need active monitoring.
steps.tx: First-line systemic therapy for intermediate and poor-risk metastatic clear cell RCC combines dual immunotherapy with **nivolumab plus ipilimumab** (paired checkpoint blockade) or a **VEGFR-TKI** (vessel-blocking tyrosine kinase inhibitor) with an anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 partner such as **pembrolizumab**. In this population combinations outperform single-agent sunitinib on survival, while immune-related toxicities need proactive monitoring.

rows: VEGFR-TKI with anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 such as pembrolizumab
Single-agent sunitinib on survival in intermediate and poor risk

steps.say: High risk disease after complete removal needs further treatment. Pembrolizumab for one year lengthens the time without recurrence in high risk clear cell cancer, as the KEYNOTE-564 trial showed. It remains the only adjuvant option with this strength of evidence.
steps.tx: **Adjuvant pembrolizumab** (postoperative immunotherapy) for **1 year** (one year) extends recurrence-free survival after resection of high-risk clear cell carcinoma, proven in the **KEYNOTE-564** trial (randomised adjuvant pembrolizumab study). No other adjuvant option carries this weight of evidence, so completely resected patients with aggressive pathology are offered a year of therapy despite the immune side effect risk.

rows: KEYNOTE-564, high-risk resected clear cell RCC
Longer disease-free survival after complete resection
Aggressive pathology earns a year of therapy despite toxicity

steps.say: Not every small mass needs an operation. Frail elderly patients with tumours under three centimetres can be watched with serial scans or treated with freezing or heating probes. Biopsy first confirms what the mass is, and growth beyond set limits converts watching into treatment.
steps.tx: **Active surveillance** (serial imaging without immediate treatment) or thermal ablation by **cryoablation** (freezing probe destruction) or **radiofrequency ablation** (heating probe destruction) suits renal masses **under 3 cm** (three centimetres) in elderly, comorbid patients when competing mortality outweighs the cancer threat. A biopsy establishes the histology first, and crossing growth thresholds or patient preference converts surveillance into intervention.

rows: Growth beyond thresholds, or patient preference
